evidence.description: Datasheet identifies Datastream security lists and weekly finance data, Bloomberg supplemental turnover, Worldscope annual statements, and hand-collected voting-rights records.
evidence.quote:
The data sources and the years in which data were downloaded or obtained are as follows:

    1) We begin the sample collection procedure by identifying firms that have at least two
       classes of shares according to the Datastream country lists during the period of 1995 to
       2007. Hyun A Hong downloaded the list of firms’ securities across countries from
       Datastream in 2008.
    2) For each share class, she extracted Friday-to-Friday weekly finance data from Datastream
       for the following variables. If the value of turnover was missing from Datastream, it was
       manually collected from Bloomberg (Doidge [2004]). All these data downloads occurred
       in 2009. In addition, she collected lagged annual financial statement variables from
       Worldscope in 2009.
    3) Because data on the number of voting rights attached to the superior and inferior voting
       shares for each firm are required, these data are hand-collected from Datastream
       Manuals, Moody’s International Manuals, filings with the national stock exchanges,
       firms’ annual reports, and the firm lists compiled by Doidge [2004]. In conducting this
       research she received significant support from Craig Doidge with respect to data
       collection. In addition, if the data ware not clear or not available, they were requested
       from each firm through faxes, emails, and phone calls. She collected this list of
       supplementary dual-class firms between 2008 and 2009.

evidence.description: Datasheet specifies Friday-to-Friday Datastream data, variables, the Bloomberg turnover fallback, Worldscope annual inputs, the 26-week criterion, and the stated sample size.
evidence.quote:
Step 2: The data collection procedures followed the guidelines established in Nenova [2003] and
Doidge [2004]. First, for each share class, she extracted Friday-to-Friday weekly data from
Datastream for the following variables: closing stock price, market value of all equity
outstanding, weekly return, dividends paid during the week, number of shares outstanding, and
turnover. If the value of turnover is missing from Datastream, it is obtained from Bloomberg
(Doidge [2004]). In addition, she collected lagged annual financial statement variables from
Worldscope.
Step 3: For each fiscal year, a firm was included in the sample only if it had at least 26 weekly
stock return observations.
Step 4: Because data on the number of voting rights attached to the superior and inferior voting
shares for each firm are required, these data are hand-collected from Datastream Manuals,
Moody’s International Manuals, filings with the national stock exchanges, firms’ annual reports,
and the firm lists compiled by Doidge [2004].
Step 5: The final sample consists of 3,350 firm-year observations from 449 firms across 20
countries.

evidence.quote:
Table 1A reports the number of firm-year observations, the number and percentage of firm-year observations for annual stock price crashes by industry. The
industry is defined according to the Fama-French 48 industry classification (Fama and French [1997]). The full sample comprises 449 dual-class firms from 20
countries over the period of 1995 through 2007. The sample consists of countries with dual-class stocks, which have sufficient accounting and market data from
DATASTREAM and WORLDSCOPE. Specifically, as for the non-US firms, we construct the sample by identifying all firms with dual-class shares during the
sample period from the country lists in the DATASTREAM database. As for the US firms, we construct the sample by identifying all firms with dual-class shares
from the Securities Data Company (SDC), S&P’s Compustat, the Center for Research in Security Prices (CRSP) and the Investor Responsibility Research Center
(IRRC) databases. We then confirm these firms’ share structure by checking the SEC filings and contacting each firm’s investment relationship department.
Following the prior voting premium literature, we impose the following sample criteria on the identified firms: (1) firms have at least two classes of shares with
different voting rights, (2) both share classes are publicly traded and listed on the domestic exchange, (3) the inferior voting share is not convertible into the
superior voting share, and (4) neither share class receives a fixed dividend (Nenova [2003]; Doidge [2004]). We download accounting variables from
WORLDSCOPE and COMPUSTAT North America. The market data we download from DATASTREAM and CRSP includes Friday-to-Friday weekly market
data for prices, returns, market returns, market value, dividend yields, number of shares outstanding, and turnover. In instances in which the values of turnover
are missing, we collect them from Bloomberg. We include a firm into the sample for a given fiscal year if it has at least 20 weekly observations. Finally, we
extensively hand collect data on the different voting rights associated with the superior- and inferior-voting shares (data source: documentation supplied by
Doidge [2004], Moody‘s International Manuals, and firms’ annual reports among others). We exclude firm-year observations with missing values for any
variable. Consequently, we obtain 3,350 firm-year observations from 20 countries as the final sample.

actions.description: Obtain the author-prepared inputs and verify source-product compatibility, identifier mappings, and the histories required by the supplied workflow.
steps: Request/stage the 20 author-prepared country series, Bloomberg turnover matrix, raw exchange-rate matrix, Dual_List, country/global index series, US index series, Worldscope_data, WS_EXT_INT_SMTH, the My2 industry_sample input, and the type-to-SEDOL mapping. The packaged workbook is only a one-column identifier list.

Confirm Datastream identifiers and pair/class coding, weekly Friday frequency, currency mapping and USD quote units, Bloomberg firm/date/turnover mapping, and Worldscope SEDOL/year item-code-to-alias mapping. Retain author-prepared inputs where available; do not reconstruct the hand-collected voting-rights list independently.

Verify the weekly inputs cover the code’s 1994–2007 filter and required prior-week return plus two market, US, and FX leads/lags around retained Fridays. The datasheet reports 26 observations per firm-year; reconcile the appendix’s 20-week description before fixing expected sample counts.

Verify annual SEDOL/year history for the one-year lags and five-year CFO/opacity windows. The code differences ocf/accruals and drops the first row per SEDOL twice before those five constructed values, so raw prerequisites may precede the visible rolling window; exact earliest alignment remains unknown because producers/joins are incomplete. Obtain the author’s coverage requirement rather than guessing a start year or independently rebuilding the input.

Use the frozen local Datastream, Worldscope, and CRSP product probes only as field-level candidates. The probes read one row and explicitly leave population/sample history unverified; confirm the author-schema transformations and actual product access before treating any candidate as compatible.

Request author input specifications and data for unprovided appendix branches. Treat FactSet/LionShares, Compustat Global/America, and other appendix references as source leads until the missing analysis workflow confirms exact products, fields, sample, and dates.
validation: After a separate authorized run, confirm all prepared inputs are readable with matching identifiers/fields and the required date history, and reconcile sample counts to the author-confirmed 26- versus 20-week rule and version-specific expected outputs.

review_notes: No analysis_only scope is supported: the release has no complete author-prepared analysis dataset or completed regression inputs. SEDOL_HKW.xlsx is only an identifier list, and the SAS program itself creates My.low/My.high from absent raw/author-prepared inputs.
